item.content:encoded:
Climate, Peace and Security Fact Sheet: Somalia

发布源: Norwegian Institute of International Affairs (NUPI) --Norway | 抓取时间: 2026-11-04

Somalia continues to grapple with increasingly severe and frequent climate shocks that impede people’s livelihoods, worsen the existing humanitarian crisis and influence local conflict dynamics over access to natural resources. In November 2025, after four consecutive failed rainy seasons had affected millions of people, the Federal Government of Somalia (FGS) declared a national drought emergency. Strong El Niño conditions are forecast to bring wetter-than-usual conditions during the October–December 2026 deyr rainy season, with a high risk of floods in central and southern Somalia. Some communities experience successive periods of drought and flooding without sufficient time to recover between shocks. These adverse effects of climate change are interacting with a volatile security situation, influenced by political competition and fragmentation, as well as continued clashes with al-Shabab, which contribute to deepening an already dire humanitarian crisis.

The United Nations Security Council recognizes the adverse effects of climate change and natural disasters on Somalia’s humanitarian situation, security and stability. It has called for comprehensive risk assessments and long-term strategies to support stabilization and resilience-building. Integrating environmental and climate considerations into security and development strategies remains crucial for Somalia’s transition towards a more resilient governance structure. item.content:encoded:
ArticlesNew researchOctober 19, 2026Testing peace policies before they reach the ground

发布源: Norwegian Institute of International Affairs (NUPI) --Norway | 抓取时间: 2026-11-04

Stabilisation policies in conflict areas often produce effects nobody planned for.

In this episode, Research Professor Cedric de Coning (NUPI) is joined by Dirk Bruin and Tomas Veloz of the Center Leo Apostel for Transdisciplinary Studies at the Vrije Universiteit Brussel (CLEA). The team brings together political science, mathematics and computational modelling.

They discussThe Adaptive Peace Simulation(APS). The aim of the tool is to help policy makers and researchers to test the effects of different policy choices in a simulated, computational version of a conflict system before committing actual resources or exposing real populations, to the risks of stabilisation interventions.

“Without this kind of modelling, you would try something, and after a couple of months you would discover the unintended consequences,” says Cedric de Coning in the podcast episode.

Tune in to listen to de Coning Bruin and Veloz discuss the science behind the tool, its development and results thus far in the process.

item.content:encoded:
What is the key to lasting peace in an unpredictable world?

发布源: Norwegian Institute of International Affairs (NUPI) --Norway | 抓取时间: 2026-11-04

PROTESTS:A resident holds a placard reading ''MONUSCO get out without delay'' as they protest against the United Nations peacekeeping force (MONUSCO) deployed in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, in Goma. Demonstrators said they were protesting against the rise of insecurity and inaction of the UN in the region.

Today's conflicts are protracted, unpredictable and complex. Yet for decades, much of international peacebuilding has relied on one-size-fits-all solutions. The thinking behind this has been that experts – peacebuilders – can identify the cause of a conflict and then prescribe ready-made solutions, often based on measures that have worked in conflicts elsewhere.

But building peace is not like building a house, where you can follow a blueprint and put up one plank at a time according to a set timeline. That is the warning from the researchers behind the new bookThe Adaptive Peacebuilding Guidebook(de Coning, Tsuchiya and Muto, 2026), whichlaunches on 2 October. Peacebuilding is more like gardening. You can fertilise, water and weed, but in the end you must let the garden grow at its own pace.

The new book offers practical, concrete advice on an approach to peacebuilding that recognises that every conflict is complex and unique. The approach is called Adaptive Peacebuilding. Being adaptive means being flexible. Throughout the process, you keep learning from the feedback your efforts generate, and continuously adjust what you do based on those lessons.

Our focus is on mobilization for human rights and access to justice for poor and marginalized groups.

We are at the forefront of research on how law and legal institutions work, and the strategic use of law as a political tool (lawfare).

As a key partner in theCentre on Law and SocialTransformation, we are developing new and better methods for assessing effects of lawfare.

We study how political institutions, political processes  and political action shape and are shaped by democracy and rights, economic outcomes and social development.

Rule of law, civil liberties and basic political rights are under threat in countries worldwide.

Our research focuses on the growing pressure against democratic institutions in Africa. We have cooperated closely with African partners for decades and have extensive fieldwork experience.

Our research holds high academic quality and provides concrete input to actors engaged in bilateral work, and to donors and activists navigating the shrinking space for civil society.
